title: Child online protection is shifting from blocking risk toward building accessible reporting, help-seeking and referral pathways
source_unit: ITU and Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children, Protection through Online Participation (PoP) Principles
geography: Global child online protection systems involving governments, industry, civil society, child helplines, academia and international organizations

denominator.unit: global Protection through Online Participation Principles

purpose.value: the Principles provide global guidance to strengthen online reporting and support systems for children

protection_route.value: online participation is treated as a route through which children can report harm, seek help, access support and be referred to protection services

design_shift.value: digital environments are framed as both spaces where risks arise and entry points for protection

observations.method: Global guidance developed by ITU and the UN Special Representative on Violence against Children with partner input and child consultations.
observations.uncertainty: The publication page describes principles and intended pathways, not implementation coverage, service quality, reporting prevalence or child outcomes across countries.
observations.subgroup: Children, adolescents, parents and caregivers, child helplines, schools, platforms, governments, social services and protection providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Expanding online reporting can improve access while increasing surveillance, false reports, retraumatization, privacy exposure or referral burden if systems are not safe and responsive.

observations.period: 2026 publication; child-centred reporting and support design

access.value: the Principles aim to support safer, more accessible and child-centred online protection pathways

agency.value: children’s online participation is treated as a potential source of help-seeking and agency, not only exposure to harm

referral.value: online reports are expected to connect to appropriate support and protection services rather than remain isolated platform events

observations.method: Principles-oriented design guidance for online reporting, support and referral systems.
observations.uncertainty: The public description does not specify universal accessibility standards, response times, safeguarding protocols or referral success measures.
observations.subgroup: Children with different ages, abilities, languages, devices, connectivity, family support and exposure to violence or exploitation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Child-centred systems require meaningful agency and informed consent; simply adding a reporting button does not ensure safety, trust, comprehension or remedy.

denominator.unit: partner and institutional actor categories identified on the publication page

partners.value: development involved civil society, academia, child helplines, industry, international organizations and UN child-violence leadership

responsibility.value: online protection is positioned as a shared pathway requiring coordination between platforms, services, governments and civil society

institutional_link.value: platform reporting is connected to public or community protection systems rather than treated as a standalone product feature

observations.method: Multi-stakeholder guidance process with child consultations and expertise from protection, technology, civil-society and international actors.
observations.uncertainty: The page does not document the representativeness of consultations, actor power, country adoption, implementation responsibilities or accountability for referral failure.
observations.subgroup: Children and families, platforms, helplines, social workers, educators, police and justice systems, regulators, civil society and international organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared responsibility can improve coordination but can also diffuse accountability when a child’s report crosses platform, state and service boundaries.

observations.period: 2026 publication; online participation as protection infrastructure

risk_and_support.value: the same digital environments can generate risk and provide an entry point to support

system_requirement.value: effective protection requires accessible reporting, trusted response and appropriate referral beyond content moderation alone

policy_scope.value: the Principles are intended for governments, industry, civil society and other actors building child-centred online protection pathways

observations.method: Policy guidance translating child online participation and protection concerns into system-level reporting and support pathways.
observations.uncertainty: The Principles are not an incident census, platform audit, clinical evaluation or proof that online participation improves child safety in practice.
observations.subgroup: Children and young people, especially those with limited offline access to help, alongside caregivers, platforms and protection institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Online access may expand help-seeking for some children while excluding others through connectivity, literacy, disability, surveillance by abusers or lack of trusted adults.

related_sources.claim: Official ITU publication page for the PoP Principles, including purpose, partner development and child-centred pathway framing.
UN Special Representative on Violence against Children institutional context.

boundary: This record adds a child-protection and digital-participation route linking online risk, child agency, reporting, help-seeking, support, referral, platform responsibility and public protection systems. It is global policy guidance, not an implementation inventory, incident prevalence estimate, child-level dataset, platform audit, service-quality evaluation or proof that online reporting produces safer outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ITU publication page was reviewed for the PoP Principles’ purpose, dual risk-and-support framing, child consultations, partner categories, child-centred accessibility and reporting-to-referral pathway claims.
